A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same state-annotated tool-graph research, renamed from SIT-Graph to H-EPM and extended in v2. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–F are available and included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, online-memory experiments on ACEBench, and component and retrieval ablations in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds model evaluations, reinforcement-learning comparisons, sensitivity experiments, entropy measurements and computational-cost results.

M1.justification: The renamed method retains the graph-based adaptive inference design. v2 substantially extends it to memory-guided GRPO training, including probabilistic skipping of procedural suggestions, memory updates during training, and masking or discarding added guidance during policy optimization (Section 4.3; Appendix C.5).

E1.justification: The four benchmark families and ACEBench's online-memory scenario are retained. v2 additionally reports RL transfer experiments, but Section 5.1 describes τ-Bench as Telecom for evaluation and Retail for training, without clearly matching these subsets to the result tables. The PDFs do not reliably establish whether additional domain/task data are introduced or only the learning and evaluation design changes.

E2.justification: v2 introduces a substantial RL comparison against standard GRPO, SFT on successful H-EPM trajectories, and AgentEvolver (Table 3). The original inference comparators—base models, ReasoningBank, ToolNet and retrieval—and the GNN4Plan ablation are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-4B/8B inference configurations, evaluates the method directly with GPT-5.1, and introduces GRPO training on 500 tasks for one epoch, with batch size 8 and eight rollouts per task. New controlled protocols vary candidate counts, summarization strategies and RL guidance. The original benchmark metrics and approximately 800/200 ToolSandbox split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component, efficiency and graph-traversal ablations are retained. v2 adds candidate-count and weight-parameter sensitivity, a 30-trajectory entropy analysis, implicit versus explicit summarization, RL skip-rate comparisons, half versus all guided rollouts, and masking versus discarding guidance (Tables 3–5 and 7–10). Figure 4 also adds a detailed trajectory case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's training rollout counts and entropy-analysis sample size describe data collection; they do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting for the performance estimates.

E6.justification: The retained GPT-4 inference scores, ACEBench results and original ablation values are unchanged. Substantial new entries include Qwen evaluations, GPT-5.1 with H-EPM, RL comparisons and supplementary analyses. For example, v2 Table 2 newly reports GPT-5.1 with H-EPM at 0.921 on τ²-Bench alongside the retained 0.842 base score. v1's GPT-5.1 ACEBench scores, 0.433 end-to-end and 0.674 process accuracy, are removed.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 revises the stated weight definition from successful tool-pair invocations to successful trajectories containing the transition, explicitly indexing the reciprocal-length sum by trajectory. Section 3 also replaces set-union history updates with ordered histories. These are limited formal revisions; no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion expand from improved inference-time tool use to experience-driven policy learning through RL. v2 adds claims of improved long-horizon exploration and generalization to unseen tasks and tools without domain-specific experience collection, together with quantified inference and out-of-distribution RL improvement claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of RL exploration versus experience reuse, domain-dependent skip rates, possible SFT overfitting, candidate-count noise, and summarization speed–accuracy tradeoffs. Appendix F identifies weaker adherence to external guidance as a limitation of stronger reasoning models. v1 discusses smaller-model benefits but lacks these RL interpretations and the specific adherence limitation.

D1.justification: Appendices C–E supply previously missing retrieval details, including all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and cosine similarity, exact summarization prompts, invocation and context-handling rules, and initial-memory collection procedures. They also document RL hyperparameters, hardware and timing. These substantially improve reproducibility; newly disclosed inference details do not establish that retained experiments were changed or rerun.

R1.justification: v1 positions its method as avoiding SFT/RL training costs; v2 positions it as improving experience reuse and exploration within RL. It introduces a substantive contrast with AgentEvolver and adds GRPO/DeepSeekMath and HybridFlow references. RLFactory and Hou et al. are dropped, while the existing tool-graph and graph-memory discussions are retained in Appendix A.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, renames the method, and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, formulation and methodology around hybrid memory and learning. Related work and experiments are reorganized, with graph-related discussions and ACEBench moved to appendices. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, with resized and relocated displays. v1 Figures 2 and 3 become v2 Figures 1 and 2, while v1 Figure 1 moves to Appendix B as Figure 3. Tables 1 and 4 expand, the GPT-5.1 comparison is restructured, and new RL/analysis tables and trajectory Figure 4 substantially extend the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves v1's deferred GPT-5.1 method evaluation through a same-backbone comparison, supplies critical missing implementation details, and adds controls that test retrieval and RL design choices. These changes substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential support beyond merely expanding scope. Unclear benchmark-domain mappings and incorrect appendix cross-references limit precision, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the gains.
